title: Causal Graphs with Latent Confounders and Post-treatment Selection
one_liner: The paper shows how to recover the true causal links when both hidden confounders and selective filtering after interventions are present.
lead: Finding causal links (what causes what) is hard. Intervention experiments help by creating changes you control, which reveal causation. But in the real world two hidden traps exist: unmeasured factors that influence multiple variables simultaneously, and selective filtering of samples after the experiment runs (a biologist keeps only healthy cells; a trial keeps only compliant subjects). The filtering trap is often overlooked. This paper introduces a new way to spot and separate causal links from selection bias, allowing recovery of the true graph structure despite both traps, by watching how each mechanism reacts differently to interventions.

problem.h2: Two hidden traps in causal discovery
paras: When scientists run experiments (called interventions), they often filter the data afterward. A biologist measures gene expression, but only keeps cells that meet quality thresholds. A medical trial runs, but only healthy enough subjects complete it. This post-treatment filtering is invisible in the data, yet it fools causal discovery algorithms.

The naive approach: look at which variables change when you intervene on one variable, then infer causation. But filtering creates spurious patterns that look like causation. If the filter favors high values, and a hidden factor pushes values up, changing one variable seems to change another, even though there is no direct causal link between them.

Existing methods cannot tell the difference between a true causal link and a false one created by selective filtering after intervention. They also struggle with unmeasured confounders (hidden factors that influence multiple variables simultaneously).

callout.html: Selective filtering after intervention creates spurious dependencies that masquerade as causal links.

steps.text: Use observational data to find which variables might be connected.
Look for conditional independence patterns (which variables become independent given others) that differ between observational and interventional data.
When a variable is intervened, true causes change their values in a specific pattern; filters create a different pattern.
Use the fingerprint to orient edges: arrows point from causes to effects, squares mark selection variables.
Output the causal structure, marked confounders, and selection indicators up to equivalence.

paras: Traditional causal discovery algorithms orient edges based solely on conditional independence patterns in data. This paper augments the graph model to include an explicit selection variable that represents post-treatment filtering, then uses differential reactions to intervention to distinguish true causal links from selection-induced spurious ones.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: distribution shift type
hidden.name: Intervention fingerprint type
paras: When you intervene on a variable, the distribution of each other variable changes. But the TYPE of change differs. A true causal child of the intervened variable changes its overall distribution (its center, spread, or shape). A variable linked only through selection changes in a narrower way: it gets filtered, but not fundamentally reshaped.

The paper estimates this by comparing conditional independence (which combinations of variables are independent of each other, given what you already know) before intervention versus after. True causal effects preserve certain independence patterns in one direction; selection effects preserve them differently. By tracking these patterns under multiple interventions, the algorithm infers which structure created them.

heat.caption: Darker means the structure produces that pattern. Highlights mark causal vs selection differences.

reads.html: When you intervene on X1, watch which other variables' distributions change and how. A true causal child changes substantially; a selection-only connection does not.
Conditional independence relations under intervention (p(k)) versus observational (p(0)) reveal which edges are causal and which are artifacts of post-treatment selection modeled as S.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: structural asymmetry under intervention
paras: A true causal link means intervening on one variable directly changes another. A hidden confounder means two variables jump together because an invisible third variable pushes both. Post-treatment selection means the sample set itself changes after intervention, creating false associations.

These three mechanisms have different structural signatures. When you intervene on a variable, a true child responds because of the direct path. A selection variable responds only if it depends on the intervened variable through other paths, creating a different pattern in the conditional independence tests. The algorithm captures these patterns from data, uses them to constrain which edge directions are possible, then applies rules that check: does this edge direction match how the actual values changed under the observed interventions? If yes, keep it; if no, flip it or mark it as selection-related.

The algorithm works in two stages. First, build an undirected skeleton using all data and a standard conditional independence test (e.g., testing if two variables remain independent given a third). Second, orient edges and add marks using rules that incorporate intervention fingerprints and selection indicators. The marks (tail, arrowhead, square for selection, circle for ambiguity) encode the equivalence class precisely.

stages.s: Observational data plus interventional experiments with selection bias
Skeleton discovery: find edges via conditional independence
Extract intervention fingerprints: how distributions shift under each intervention
Orientation: apply rules that match edge directions to fingerprints
Mark confounders and selection variables with special symbols
Causal graph with hidden confounders and post-treatment selection identified

math.h2: The core equation and worked example
math.words: When variable XA is independent of XB given (XC and selection indicator S), record that independence. Under intervention on variable XI, check if the same independence holds in the new distribution p(k). If true causes are present but selection is not, certain independencies survive intervention; selection-only connections break.
math.equation: For any k in [K], if XA ⊥ XB | {XC, S} in observational p(0), then check if XA ⊥ XB | {XC, S} holds in p(k). Mismatch indicates selection effect.
symbols: selection indicator (1 if sample kept after filtering, 0 if discarded)
data distribution after intervening on variable k
statistical independence (two things do not predict each other)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Observational data: X1 and X2 appear independent when we know sample quality is high. This pattern is recorded.
Intervene on X1 (force it to increase). In the new data: if there is a real causal link, both X1 and X2 jump together, breaking the independence. Record this change.
If selection alone created the link, then intervening on X1 only changes which samples the quality filter keeps, not X2 directly. The independence pattern changes differently.

Orientation rule: the independence breaks under intervention indicates causation. The independence breaks in a different way indicates selection. Real causal effects remain predictable through selection changes; selection effects are unpredictable.

math.note: The independence tests detect which graph structures could have generated the observed data; the intervention fingerprints pin down which structures actually did.

charts.title: Naive interventional discovery (ignores selection bias)
charts.note: Without modeling selection, many true links are missed and false spurious links are created.

charts.title: F-FCI (explicit selection model)
charts.note: By tracking intervention fingerprints, the method separates real causation from selection artifacts.

items.html: If the filtering rule is completely hidden and independent of causal structure, no algorithm can recover it from data alone. F-FCI assumes the selection rule is not adversarially hidden.

If you only intervene on a few variables, you miss fingerprint patterns that distinguish selection from causation because the algorithm relies on comparing how patterns change across multiple intervention types. Each intervention creates a new fingerprint; more interventions build a richer signature that only true causal structures can match.
If many latent confounders exist and are densely connected, the equivalence class (set of possible graphs) grows large. The method may identify multiple structures that fit equally well.

With observational data plus multiple interventions and reasonable selection structure (e.g., selection depends only on observed variables or the intervened one), F-FCI recovers the true graph up to the fine-grained equivalence class.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a synthetic graph with a known causal structure (e.g., variable A causes B which causes C, plus a hidden factor that pushes both A and B). Add a selection rule that filters high values based on B and the hidden factor. Generate observational data, then interventional data (intervene on each variable one at a time, then apply the selection filter). Run F-FCI on the data. Confirm: the algorithm outputs the correct causal edges, marks the hidden confounder, and identifies the selection pattern. Compare to naive algorithms that ignore selection, which produce many false links.
demo.metric_eq: Precision and recall of recovered edges, precision of identified confounders, and precision of selection structure detection.
demo.closing: The demo must show that a realistic selection filter (filtering by a noisy quality score) creates false links that fool standard algorithms but not F-FCI.
